newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: British scientist dismisses polar meltdown threat.
newsitem.headline: British scientist dismisses polar meltdown threat.

text.p: A prominent British scientist on Wednesday dismissed as irrelevant fears that global warming could melt large quantities of Antarctic ice and cause world sea levels to rise sharply.

British Antarctic Survey member David Vaughan told a world meterological conference in Australia it would take 200 years at current warming rates before the problem would be serious. "It is very unlikely that the warming trend in the Antarctic Peninsula could be sustained for that length of time without very major changes elsewhere which would make this (issue) seem rather irrelevant," Vaughan told the Melbourne conference.
Vaughan said scientists were far more concerned about the effects of oceanographic conditions on the mass of southerly ice shelves and even the possibility these shelves would thicken.
The melting of polar ice caps is cited by many scientists as one of the most dangerous effects of global warming.

The Inter-Governmental Panel on Climate Change, set up by governments to investigate global warming, has said that many small island states could be wiped out by anticipated rises in world sea levels.
The Antarctic coastline is surrounded by shelves of ice wherever there are bays or islands to constrain them.
The focus of scientific studies of these shelves has been a peninsula on the west coast called the Western Peninsula.
Over the past 50 years scientists have detected a strong warming trend at the Western Peninsula totalling about 2.5 degrees Celsius (4.5 degrees Farenheit).
Last year environmental group Greenpeace released pictures of cracks in one of the Western Peninsula's ice shelves, after an expedition by its MV Artic Sunrise vessel.
Greenpeace said the cracks suggested the collapse of the Larsen B shelf was imminent and was further evidence that global warming could be affecting the Antarctic.
Vaughan said he disagreed with the Greenpeace assessment of the cracks and said there were other examples of this phenomenon in the Antarctic.
"These chasms (cracks) have been known to last as long as 50 years before icebergs were formed," he said.
